source: Marqu - The Hebrew Gospel of Mark v1.2

verses.translation: And as{H834} they were going out{H3318} from the sanctuary{H4720}, one{H259} of his disciples{H8527} said{H559} to him: Rabbi{H7227}, see{H7200} these buildings{H1146} and what{H335} stones{H68}!

one_way_hebrew: Uses המקדש (ha-miqdash, H4720 — 'the sanctuary') — the OT term for the sacred precinct (Ex 25:8, 1 Kgs 6:16, Ezek 37:26). Greek ἱερόν ('temple') is the broader term for the entire complex. A back-translator would more likely use בית המקדש ('house of the sanctuary'). The Hebrew uses the specific sacred-space word.
translation_notes: תלמידיו (talmidav — 'his disciples') is post-biblical Hebrew, from the root למד (lamad — 'to learn'). No standard Strong's number.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} answered{H6030} and said{H559}: Do you see{H7200} these great{H1419} buildings{H1146}? Not a stone{H68} shall remain{H7604} upon a stone{H68} that shall not be torn down{H2040}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תהרס (tehares — 'shall be torn down', H2040) — the same verb used for the destruction of pagan altars (Judg 6:25, Ex 34:13) and the undoing of divine constructions (Jer 45:4). Greek καταλυθῇ ('shall be dissolved/destroyed') is more generic. A back-translator would use תחרב or תשחת, not the altar-demolition verb הרס.

verses.translation: And as he sat{H3427} on the Mount{H2022} of Olives{H2132}, opposite{H5048} the sanctuary{H4720}, Kefa{H3710} and Ya'aqov{H3290} and Yochanan{H3110} and Andrei asked{H7592} him in secret{H5475}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בסוד (be-sod, H5475 — 'in secret/counsel'). This is the OT term for intimate divine counsel (Jer 23:18,22 — 'who has stood in the sod of YHWH?'; Ps 25:14 — 'the sod of YHWH is for those who fear him'; Amos 3:7). Greek κατ' ἰδίαν ('privately') is merely spatial. The Hebrew frames this as a prophetic sod-session — the disciples entering Yeshua's inner counsel circle, just as prophets enter YHWH's sod. A back-translator from Greek would use בסתר or לבד, not the prophetic sod.
greek_deviations: Greek lists Peter, James, John, and Andrew (same four). No divergence in names, but the Hebrew's סוד framing is absent from Greek.
textual_notes: The four disciples mirror the first four called (Mark 1:16-20). The 'secret counsel' session on the Mount of Olives echoes Zechariah 14:4 where YHWH stands on the Mount of Olives.

verses.translation: Tell{H559} us, when{H4970} shall these things{H1697} be{H1961}, and what is the sign{H226} when shall be the end{H7093} of the world{H5769}, when all{H3605} things{H1697} shall begin to perish{H6461}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses ליפסד (le-yifased — 'to perish/spoil/decay') — a distinctly Hebraic verb from the root פסד ('to rot/corrupt'), used in rabbinic Hebrew for food spoiling and moral decay. Greek συντελεῖσθαι means 'to be completed/consummated.' These are OPPOSITE concepts — the Hebrew asks when things will ROT; the Greek asks when things will be COMPLETED. A back-translator from Greek would never produce פסד.

Uses הקץ (ha-qets — 'the end', H7093) — the eschatological term from Daniel 8:17, 11:35,40, 12:4,9,13. Greek συντέλεια ('completion') is related but distinct. The Hebrew directly invokes Daniel's apocalyptic vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the end of the world when all things shall begin to PERISH.' Greek: 'the sign of your coming and the COMPLETION of the age.' The Hebrew frames the eschaton as decay; the Greek as fulfillment. Entirely different eschatological perspectives.
Hebrew has a single question about the 'end of the world.' Greek has TWO distinct questions: (1) when shall these things be, and (2) what is the sign of the completion. The Hebrew conflates them.
translation_notes: 'Perish' for yifased — preserving the unique Hebrew concept of cosmic decay/rotting, absent from the Greek.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} answering{H6030} began{H2490} to say{H559}: See{H7200}! Look{H5027}! That no{H3808} one{H376} deceive{H3238} you.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יונה (yoneh — 'oppress/deceive', H3238 from ינה) — the Torah verb for oppressing the stranger (Ex 22:20, Lev 19:33, 25:14,17). Greek πλανήσῃ ('lead astray') is about deception. The Hebrew warns against OPPRESSION, not mere deception — someone who would exploit and cheat them. A back-translator from Greek would use יתעה or ירמה, not the stranger-oppression verb.

verses.translation: For many{H7227} shall come{H935} into the world{H5769} in my name{H8034}, saying{H559} that I am he{H1931}, and many{H7227} shall they deceive{H7411}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לעולם (la-olam — 'into the world/into eternity', H5769). Greek simply says ἐλεύσονται ('shall come'). The Hebrew adds 'into the world' — a characteristic Hebrew idiom for entering earthly existence, absent from the Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'saying that I am he' (שאני הוא). Greek: 'saying ἐγώ εἰμι (I AM).' Both preserve the echo of Exodus 3:14, but the Hebrew adds שאני ('that I') as a reporting clause.

verses.translation: But when you see{H7200} many{H7227} wars{H4421} or beginnings of wars{H4421}, do not fear{H3372}, for this is required{H2326} to be{H1961}, but the end{H7093} is not yet{H5750}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'many wars or BEGINNINGS of wars.' Greek: 'wars and RUMORS of wars' (ἀκοὰς πολέμων). Hebrew says 'beginnings' — wars starting; Greek says 'rumors' — reports about wars. Different concepts entirely.

verses.translation: And peoples{H5971} shall rise{H6965} against{H5048} peoples{H5971}, and king{H4428} against{H5048} king{H4428}, and there shall be{H1961} earthquakes{H7494} in the land{H776}, and famine{H7458}, and the beginning of sorrows{H3511} they shall be{H1961}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מלך נגד מלך (melekh neged melekh — 'king against king', H4428 singular). Greek has βασιλεία ἐπὶ βασιλείαν ('kingdom against kingdom'). Hebrew speaks of KINGS (persons in conflict); Greek speaks of KINGDOMS (political entities at war). A back-translator from Greek 'kingdom' would write ממלכה נגד ממלכה, not 'king against king.' The Hebrew personalizes the conflict — wars originate from rulers, not abstractions.

Uses כאבים (ke'avim — 'sorrows/pains', H3511) — physical labor-pain language (Jer 22:23, Job 33:19). Greek ὠδίνων ('birth-pangs') shares the birth imagery but the Hebrew root כאב is broader, encompassing all physical suffering. Isaiah 13:8 uses חבלים for birth-pangs; this author chose a different pain word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'king against king.' Greek: 'kingdom against kingdom.' Singular vs. abstract.
Hebrew adds 'in the land' (בארץ) for earthquakes. Greek has 'in various places' (κατὰ τόπους).

verses.translation: Then guard{H8104} yourselves, for they shall lead{H3212} you [to their councils] and in the houses{H1004} of their assemblies they shall strike{H5221} you; and you shall stand{H5975} before{H6440} the kings{H4428} and the rulers{H8269} to bring{H935} testimony{H5715} of me in their witness.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בתי כנסיותיהם (batei kenisyoteihem — 'houses of their assemblies') — the compound Hebrew construction for synagogues using the native word כנסיה ('gathering/assembly'). Greek has συναγωγάς, a Greek calque of the same concept. The Hebrew uses a COMPOUND phrase ('houses of assembly') where the Greek has a single word. A back-translator would use בתי כנסת (the standard term), not this longer construction.

Uses שרים (sarim — 'rulers/princes', H8269) — the OT title for tribal/military/administrative leaders (Gen 12:15, Dan 10:13,20). Greek ἡγεμόνων ('governors') is a Roman administrative title. A back-translator from Greek would use פחות (pachot — 'governors') as in Ezra 8:36, not the Israelite sarim.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'to bring testimony OF ME in their witness.' Greek: 'as a testimony TO THEM' (εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς). The Hebrew says the testimony is ABOUT Yeshua; the Greek says it is directed AT them.
translation_notes: מועצותיהם (mo'atsoteihem — 'their councils') is post-biblical, from עצה (etsah — counsel, H6098).

verses.translation: And it is required{H2326} first{H7223} to proclaim{H1875} the kingdom{H4438} of heaven{H8064} to all{H3605} the peoples{H5971}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses המלכות שממיי (ha-malkhut she-mi-shamayim — 'the kingdom of heaven', H4438+H8064). Greek has τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ('the gospel/good-news'). These are ENTIRELY different concepts. Hebrew says the KINGDOM OF HEAVEN must be proclaimed; Greek says the GOSPEL must be preached. A back-translator from Greek would write הבשורה ('the good-news'), not 'the kingdom of heaven.' This is among the strongest one-way markers in Mark 13 — the Hebrew author's concept of what must be spread to all nations is the REIGN OF HEAVEN, not a message about events.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the kingdom of heaven.' Greek: 'the gospel' (τὸ εὐαγγέλιον). Completely different object of proclamation.
Hebrew: 'to all the peoples' (לכל העמים). Greek: 'to all the nations' (εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη). Hebrew עמים and Greek ἔθνη overlap but עמים carries a more neutral 'peoples' connotation.

verses.translation: And when they lead{H5090} you captive{H8610}, do not fear{H6342} what you shall say{H559}; you shall speak{H1696} as the Holy{H6918} Spirit{H7307} directs{H3474} you in that hour{H8160} — you shall not speak{H1696}, but the Holy{H6918} Spirit{H7307} on your behalf.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הקדוש רוח (ha-qadosh ruach — 'the Holy Spirit') with adjective BEFORE noun — unusual Hebrew word order. The standard OT form is רוח הקדש (ruach ha-qodesh — 'spirit of holiness', Isa 63:10-11, Ps 51:13). Greek τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον follows standard Greek with article-noun-article-adjective. This reversed order is characteristic of later Sephardic Hebrew and could not derive from the Greek word order.

Uses יישרכם (yeyashrekhem — 'directs/guides you straight', H3474 from ישר). Greek δοθῇ ('shall be given'). The Hebrew says the Spirit will STRAIGHTEN/DIRECT them; the Greek says words will be GIVEN to them. Different models of inspiration — Hebrew: guidance; Greek: dictation.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Holy Spirit directs you.' Greek: 'it is not you who speak but the Holy Spirit.' The Hebrew frames it as GUIDANCE; the Greek as REPLACEMENT of the speaker.

verses.translation: And a brother{H251} shall deliver{H4560} his brother{H251} to death{H4194}, and the father{H1} the son{H1121}, and children{H1121} shall rise{H6965} against their father{H1} and against their mothers{H517} and oppress{H5065} them to death{H4194}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses וינגשום (ve-yingshu-m — 'and shall oppress them', H5065) — the specific verb for tyrannical oppression of laborers and the downtrodden (Ex 3:7, Isa 3:12, 14:2). Greek θανατώσουσιν αὐτούς ('shall put them to death') simply means 'kill.' The Hebrew says they will OPPRESS them to death — a slow grinding persecution, not a quick execution. A back-translator from Greek would use ימיתום ('shall kill them').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall oppress them to death' (lingering persecution). Greek: 'shall put them to death' (execution).
Hebrew mentions 'mothers' (אמותם, plural). Greek has only 'parents' (γονεῖς). Hebrew specifies the maternal relationship.
textual_notes: Echoes Micah 7:6 — 'For the son treats the father with contempt, the daughter rises up against her mother.' The Hebrew preserves the Micah framework of familial betrayal.

verses.translation: And all{H3605} shall rage{H7107}, and the one who endures{H8552} to the end{H7093} shall be saved{H3467}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יקציפו (yaqtsifu — 'shall rage/be furious', H7107) — the verb for divine and human wrath (Deut 1:34, 9:19; Eccl 5:5). Greek μισούμενοι ('being hated') is passive reception of hatred. Hebrew: the world will RAGE; Greek: you will be HATED. Active fury vs. passive endurance. A back-translator from Greek would write שנואים ('hated'), not the active wrath verb קצף.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'all shall rage' (active). Greek: 'you shall be hated by all' (passive). Reversed grammatical perspective.

verses.translation: And when you see{H7200} the desolating{H8074} abomination{H8251} standing{H5975} in a place{H4725} that is not fitting{H7200} — let the one who reads{H7121} understand{H995} — then those in Yehudah{H3063} shall flee{H5127} to the mountains{H2022}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses השקוץ שומם (ha-shiquts shomem — 'the desolating abomination', H8251+H8074) — this is the EXACT phrase from Daniel 12:11 (שקוץ שומם) and closely parallels Daniel 9:27 (שקוצים משומם) and Daniel 11:31 (השקוץ משומם). Greek βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως ('the abomination of desolation') is a loose rendering that converts the Hebrew active participle שומם ('desolating') into a Greek genitive noun ('of desolation'). A back-translator from Greek would likely write תועבת השממה or שקוץ השממה — using a noun construct, not Daniel's exact participial form. The Hebrew preserves Daniel's precise grammar.

Uses עמוד (omod — 'standing', H5975) — a masculine participle. Greek ἑστηκότα is also masculine, but the Hebrew participle specifically echoes Daniel 12:11 where the abomination is SET UP (הנתן). The Hebrew envisions the abomination as a standing figure — possibly an idol or statue erected in sacred space.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'standing in a place that is not fitting' (שאין ראוי). Greek: 'standing where it ought not' (ὅπου οὐ δεῖ). Similar meaning but the Hebrew ראוי ('fitting/worthy') has a stronger moral/ritual valence than Greek δεῖ ('it is necessary').
translation_notes: 'Desolating abomination' preserves Daniel's participial grammar — the abomination actively desolates, it is not merely 'of desolation.'
textual_notes: Daniel 12:11: וּמֵעֵת הוּסַר הַתָּמִיד וְלָתֵת שִׁקּוּץ שֹׁמֵם — 'And from the time the continual offering is removed and the desolating abomination is set up.' The Hebrew Gospel preserves Daniel's exact phrase.

verses.translation: And whoever is on the upper-room{H5944} shall not go down{H3381} to the house{H1004}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עלייה (aliyah, H5944 — 'upper room/roof chamber') — the specific architectural term for the rooftop room in Israelite houses (2 Kgs 4:10 — Elisha's upper room; Judg 3:20-25 — Eglon's upper room; 2 Sam 18:33 — David's upper room). Greek δώματος ('housetop/roof') is the external roof surface. Hebrew specifies a ROOM; Greek specifies a ROOF. A back-translator from Greek 'roof' would use גג (gag — 'roof'), not the upper-room term.

verses.translation: And the one who is in the field{H7704} shall not turn{H7725} back{H268} to take{H3947} his garment{H899}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'his garment' (בגדו, singular). Greek: 'his garments' (τὸ ἱμάτιον αὐτοῦ, singular also). Agreement here.

verses.translation: And woe{H1945} to those who are pregnant{H2030} and to those nursing{H3243} in those days{H3117}!
Entreat{H2470} the face{H6440} of God{H410} that this not come{H935} in the time{H6256} of the cold{H7135}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חלו פני האל (chalu penei ha-El — 'entreat the face of God', H2470+H6440+H410). This is a SPECIFIC OT idiom: חלה את פני ה' (Ex 32:11, 1 Sam 13:12, 1 Kgs 13:6, 2 Chr 33:12, Jer 26:19, Zech 8:21-22, Mal 1:9). Greek προσεύχεσθε ('pray') is generic. No back-translator from 'pray' would produce this specific three-word OT formula. The Hebrew author uses the covenantal prayer idiom — literally 'making God's face sweet.'

CRITICAL: Uses הקור (ha-qor — 'the cold', H7135). Greek χειμῶνος means 'winter' (the season). The Hebrew says 'the cold' — a weather condition, not a calendar season. Matthew's parallel adds 'nor on a Shabbat' (μηδὲ σαββάτῳ) which the Hebrew Mark lacks. The Hebrew concern is practical (cold weather for refugees in mountains) rather than calendrical.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'entreat the face of God' (specific OT prayer formula). Greek: 'pray' (generic).
Hebrew: 'in the time of the cold.' Greek: 'in winter.' Weather vs. season.
translation_notes: 'Entreat the face' preserves the OT idiom חלה פנים — literally to make the face sweet/favorable, the posture of supplication before a king or God.

verses.translation: For in that time{H6256} there shall be{H1961} more distress{H6869} in the world{H5769} than ever{H5769} was, from the day{H3117} the Name{H8034} created{H1254} the world{H5769} until now{H6258}, and there shall not be{H1961} after it.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses השם (ha-Shem — 'the Name') as a substitute for the divine name. This is a characteristically Jewish practice of reverential circumlocution (Lev 24:11,16). Greek has ὁ θεός ('God'). A back-translator from Greek would write אלהים ('God'), not the reverential השם. This substitution appears repeatedly in the Hebrew Mark and is a strong marker of Jewish authorial practice.

Uses שברא (she-bara — 'created', H1254) — the verb reserved exclusively for DIVINE creation in the OT (Gen 1:1,21,27, 2:3; Isa 40:26, 42:5). Greek ἔκτισεν is also 'created' but the Hebrew ברא carries the specific theological weight of creation ex nihilo. The combination 'the Name created the world' uses both Jewish reverential practice and Torah creation vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Name created the world' (השם). Greek: 'God created the creation' (ὁ θεὸς ἔκτισεν τὴν κτίσιν). The use of 'the Name' vs. 'God' is a fundamental divergence in divine reference.
Hebrew uses צרה (tsarah — 'distress/trouble', H6869). Greek uses θλῖψις ('tribulation/pressure'). The Hebrew term echoes 'the time of Jacob's trouble' (עֵת צָרָה, Jer 30:7; Dan 12:1).
textual_notes: Daniel 12:1: וְהָיְתָה עֵת צָרָה אֲשֶׁר לֹא נִהְיְתָה מִהְיוֹת גּוֹי עַד הָעֵת הַהִיא — 'And there shall be a time of distress such as never was since there was a nation until that time.' The Hebrew Mark echoes Daniel's exact language (עת צרה).

verses.translation: And if the Name{H8034} does not shorten{H7114} that time{H2166}, no flesh{H1320} shall be saved{H3467}; but for the sake of the chosen{H972} whom he chose{H977}, he shall shorten{H7114} the days{H3117}.

one_way_hebrew: Again uses השם (ha-Shem — 'the Name') for God — second occurrence in two verses, confirming this is the author's consistent practice, not a one-off choice.

Uses כל בשר (kol basar — 'all flesh', H3605+H1320) — the OT phrase for all living creatures (Gen 6:12,13,17,19; 7:15,16,21; 9:11,15,16,17; Isa 40:5,6, 49:26, 66:23). Greek πᾶσα σάρξ is a direct calque. Both traditions preserve the phrase, but the Hebrew is the original idiom.

verses.translation: And then if any{H335} man{H376} says{H559} to you: See{H2009}, the Anointed{H4899} is here{H6311}! See{H2009}, the Anointed{H4899} is there{H8033}! — do not believe{H539}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses משיח (mashiach — 'anointed', H4899) — the OT term for one anointed with oil (1 Sam 2:10, 16:6, 24:7; Ps 2:2, 132:17; Dan 9:25-26). Greek Χριστός is a translation of this. Both converge here, but the Hebrew preserves the concrete physical meaning — 'smeared with oil' — while the Greek has become a proper name.

verses.translation: Then shall arise{H6965} lying{H8267} prophets{H5030}, showing{H7200} signs{H226} and wonders{H6382}, to deceive{H1819} even, if possible{H3201}, the chosen{H972}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שקרנים נביאים (shaqranim nevi'im — 'lying prophets') with the adjective BEFORE the noun. Greek has ψευδόχριστοι καὶ ψευδοπροφῆται ('false-christs AND false-prophets'). The Hebrew has only 'lying prophets' — no mention of false anointed ones. Greek adds an entire category (false christs) absent from the Hebrew.

Uses אותות ונפלאות (otot u-mofetim/nifla'ot — 'signs and wonders', H226+H6382) — the standard OT pair from Deuteronomy 13:2-4 (the test of a false prophet) and Exodus 7:3 (the plagues). The Hebrew author frames the warning in Deuteronomy's false-prophet test language.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'lying prophets' only. Greek: 'false-christs AND false-prophets.' Greek adds the 'false-christs' category.
Hebrew: 'to deceive' (לדמות). Greek: 'to deceive/lead astray' (πρὸς τὸ ἀποπλανᾶν). The Hebrew root דמה means 'to resemble/liken' — the false prophets make things SEEM like what they are not.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 13:2-4 — 'If a prophet arises among you and gives you a sign or wonder (אוֹת אוֹ מוֹפֵת), and the sign or wonder comes to pass... you shall not listen to that prophet.' The Hebrew Mark uses the exact Deuteronomy test language.

verses.translation: Guard yourselves{H8104}! I say{H559} to you before{H6924} it comes to pass{H1961}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'I say to you before it comes to pass.' Greek: 'I have told you all things beforehand' (προείρηκα ὑμῖν πάντα). Hebrew uses present tense; Greek uses perfect tense.

verses.translation: And in those days{H3117}, after that distress{H6869} has passed{H5674}, the sun{H8121} shall darken{H2821} and the moon{H3842} shall not shine{H2224}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תזריח (tazriach — 'shall shine/rise', H2224 from זרח). Greek: οὐ δώσει τὸ φέγγος αὐτῆς ('shall not give its light'). Hebrew: the moon will not RISE/SHINE (active verb of luminescence); Greek: the moon will not GIVE its light (transitive). A back-translator would use תתן אורה ('give her light'), not the sunrise verb זרח.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the moon shall not shine.' Greek: 'the moon shall not give her light.' Different framing.
textual_notes: Isaiah 13:10: כִּי כוֹכְבֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם וּכְסִילֵיהֶם לֹא יָהֵלּוּ אוֹרָם חָשַׁךְ הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בְּצֵאתוֹ וְיָרֵחַ לֹא יַגִּיהַּ אוֹרוֹ — 'The stars and their constellations shall not flash their light; the sun is darkened at its rising, and the moon shall not cause its light to shine.' Joel 2:31 also: 'The sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood.'

verses.translation: And the stars{H3556} shall fall{H5307} from the heavens{H8064}, and the powers{H3581} of the heavens{H8064} shall shake{H5128}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ינועו (yinu'u — 'shall shake/tremble/wander', H5128 from נוע) — the verb used for the shaking of trees (Isa 7:2), the trembling of the earth (1 Sam 14:15), and wandering of fugitives (Gen 4:12 — Cain's 'wandering'). Greek σαλευθήσονται ('shall be shaken') is seismic. The Hebrew verb encompasses both trembling AND dislocation — the heavenly powers not only shake but become displaced.
textual_notes: Isaiah 34:4: וְנָמַקּוּ כָּל צְבָא הַשָּׁמַיִם — 'And all the host of heaven shall rot/dissolve.' The Hebrew Mark uses a different verb (נוע rather than מקק) but the same cosmic imagery.

verses.translation: Then they shall see{H7200} the Son{H1121} of God{H433} coming{H935} from the heavens{H8064} with great{H1419} power{H3581} and light{H219}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בן האלוה (ben ha-Eloah — 'Son of God', H1121+H433). Greek has τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('the Son of MAN'). This is an ENORMOUS divergence. The Hebrew says 'Son of God' where the Greek says 'Son of Man.' No back-translator from Greek 'Son of Man' would write 'Son of God.' These are different theological claims. The Hebrew author consistently uses בן האלוה as a messianic title, whereas the Greek preserves the Daniel 7:13 'Son of Man' language. This suggests the Hebrew and Greek represent INDEPENDENT traditions about Yeshua's self-designation.

Uses ואורה (ve-orah — 'and light', H219) where Greek has δόξης πολλῆς ('much glory'). Hebrew: power and LIGHT; Greek: power and GLORY. Light (אורה) connects to the theophany traditions — God appears in light (Ps 104:2, Hab 3:4, Ezek 1:4). Glory (δόξα) is a broader concept. A back-translator from Greek would write וכבוד רב ('and much glory').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Son of GOD' (בן האלוה). Greek: 'Son of MAN' (υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου). Fundamentally different title.
Hebrew: 'power and light.' Greek: 'power and glory.' Different attributes.
Hebrew: 'coming FROM the heavens' (directional — FROM heaven downward). Greek: 'coming IN clouds' (ἐν νεφέλαις). Different imagery — descent vs. cloud-riding.
contradictions: The Son of God vs. Son of Man divergence cannot be resolved as a translation variant. It represents a fundamental difference in how the Hebrew and Greek traditions identify the eschatological figure.
translation_notes: אלוה (Eloah, H433) — the rare singular of Elohim, used primarily in Job and Deuteronomy 32. Its use here (rather than אלהים) matches the consistent pattern of the Hebrew Mark.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:13-14 (Greek context): 'One like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven.' The Greek Mark quotes Daniel directly. The Hebrew Mark reinterprets the figure as 'Son of God' — identifying Daniel's 'son of man' with divine sonship.

verses.translation: And then he shall send{H7971} his messengers{H4397} and gather{H6908} his chosen{H972} from the four{H702} wings{H3671} of the earth{H776}, from the heavens{H8064} and unto the earth{H776}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses כנפות הארץ (kanfot ha-aretz — 'wings of the earth', H3671+H776) — the specific OT idiom for the extremities of the earth (Isa 11:12 — 'the four wings of the earth'; Job 37:3, 38:13; Ezek 7:2). Greek τεσσάρων ἀνέμων ('four winds') is a completely different metaphor — winds vs. wings. A back-translator from Greek 'four winds' would write ארבע רוחות (arba ruchot), not כנפות הארץ. The Hebrew author thinks in Isaiah's geography of the earth as a garment with four corners/wings.

Uses ויקבץ (ve-yiqabets — 'and gather', H6908) — the specific verb for the regathering of Israel's exiles (Deut 30:3-4; Isa 11:12, 56:8; Jer 31:10; Ezek 20:34, 34:13, 36:24). Greek ἐπισυνάξει ('shall gather together') is adequate but lacks the exile-return resonance.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'four wings of the earth' (כנפות הארץ). Greek: 'four winds' (τεσσάρων ἀνέμων). Entirely different metaphor.
Hebrew: 'his chosen' (נבחריו). Greek: 'his elect' (ἐκλεκτοὺς αὐτοῦ). Semantic overlap but Hebrew בחר carries covenant-election weight (Deut 7:6, 14:2).
translation_notes: 'Wings of the earth' preserves the Isaiah 11:12 image — the earth conceived as a garment with four corners (kanfot), the same word used for the corners of a prayer shawl (tsitsit on the kanfot, Num 15:38).
textual_notes: Isaiah 11:12: וְנָשָׂא נֵס לַגּוֹיִם וְאָסַף נִדְחֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וּנְפֻצוֹת יְהוּדָה יְקַבֵּץ מֵאַרְבַּע כַּנְפוֹת הָאָרֶץ — 'And he shall raise a signal for the nations, and gather the outcasts of Israel, and collect the scattered of Judah from the four wings of the earth.'

verses.translation: Take{H3947} the parable{H4912} from the fig tree{H8384}: when she begins to bud{H2590} and to make{H6213} leaves{H5929}, you shall know{H3045} that the end{H7093} draws near{H7126}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לחנוט (lachanot — 'to bud/put forth early fruit', H2590 from חנט). This rare verb appears in Song of Songs 2:13: הַתְּאֵנָה חָנְטָה פַגֶּיהָ — 'the fig tree puts forth her green figs.' Greek ἁπαλὸς γένηται ('becomes tender') describes a quality; the Hebrew verb describes a PROCESS of budding/fruiting. A back-translator from Greek 'tender' would use רך (rakh), not the Song of Songs fig-budding verb.

Uses הקץ (ha-qets — 'the end') where Greek has θέρος ('summer'). MAJOR divergence: the Hebrew fig tree signals the END; the Greek fig tree signals SUMMER. The Hebrew reads this as an eschatological parable; the Greek reads it as a seasonal analogy.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the end draws near.' Greek: 'summer is near.' Different referent — eschatological end vs. agricultural season.
textual_notes: Song of Songs 2:13: הַתְּאֵנָה חָנְטָה פַגֶּיהָ — 'The fig tree has budded her early figs.' The Hebrew Mark uses this exact verb, connecting the Olivet Discourse to the love-poetry of Song of Songs.

verses.translation: Likewise, when you see{H7200} these things{H1697}, you shall know{H3045} that the end{H7093} of the world{H5769} draws near{H7126} to the door{H6607}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קץ העולם (qets ha-olam — 'end of the world') — explicitly eschatological. Greek has ἐγγύς ἐστιν ἐπὶ θύραις ('it is near, at the doors'). The Hebrew specifies WHAT is near (the end of the world); the Greek leaves the subject ambiguous ('it/he is near').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the end of the world draws near to the door' (singular). Greek: 'it is near, at the doors' (plural θύραις). Hebrew makes the eschatological referent explicit.

verses.translation: Truth{H571} I say{H559} to you, that this generation{H1755} shall not pass{H5674} until all{H3605} these things{H1697} come to pass{H935}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אמת (emet — 'truth', H571) where Greek has ἀμήν ('amen'). Greek amen is a transliteration of Hebrew אמן. But the Hebrew text does NOT use אמן; it uses אמת — a different word from the same root. A back-translator from Greek ἀμήν would write אמן, not אמת. This is a consistent pattern in the Hebrew Mark.

verses.translation: The heavens{H8064} and the earth{H776} shall pass{H5674}, but these my words{H1697} shall not pass{H5674}.

textual_notes: Isaiah 40:8: וּדְבַר אֱלֹהֵינוּ יָקוּם לְעוֹלָם — 'But the word of our God shall stand forever.' Yeshua claims for his own words the permanence Isaiah attributes to YHWH's word.

verses.translation: That day{H3117} and that hour{H8160}, none knows{H3045} — not the messengers{H4397} of the heavens{H8064}, nor the Son{H1121} — but the Father{H1}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלאכי השמים (malakhei ha-shamayim — 'messengers of the heavens') where Greek has οἱ ἄγγελοι οἱ ἐν οὐρανῷ ('the angels IN heaven'). Hebrew: messengers OF the heavens (possessive — they belong to heaven); Greek: angels IN heaven (locative — they are situated in heaven). Different prepositions signal different conceptions of angelic nature.

verses.translation: Guard yourselves{H8104} and be awake{H5782} and pray{H6419}, for you know{H3045} not the time{H2166} nor the hour{H8160}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'guard yourselves and be awake and PRAY.' Greek: 'Watch, keep alert' (ἀγρυπνεῖτε). Greek omits 'pray' here (though some manuscripts add it). The Hebrew includes the full triad: guard-wake-pray.

verses.translation: Like a man{H376} who goes{H1980} on a journey and leaves{H5800} his house{H1004} and gives{H5414} authority to his servants{H5650} and commands{H6680} the watchman to watch.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יכולת (yekhólet — 'ability/authority') — a later Hebrew abstract noun. Greek ἐξουσίαν ('authority') is standard. The Hebrew uses the capacity/ability word rather than the authority/jurisdiction word — the servants receive CAPABILITY, not just PERMISSION.

Uses שיעור (shi'ur — 'measure/watch-period') — a specifically rabbinic Hebrew term for a measured quantity or defined period of duty. No Greek equivalent; Greek has τῷ θυρωρῷ ('to the doorkeeper'). The Hebrew frames the watchman's task as a measured duty-period.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'commands the watchman to watch a measured period.' Greek: 'commands the doorkeeper to keep watch' (τῷ θυρωρῷ ἵνα γρηγορῇ). Hebrew envisions a watchman (military); Greek envisions a doorkeeper (domestic).

verses.translation: Therefore be awake{H5782}, for you do not know{H3045} the day{H3117} and the hour{H8160} — whether the master{H113} of the house{H1004} comes{H935} in the evening{H6153}, or at midnight{H2676}{H3915}, or at the rooster's call, or in the morning{H1242}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses the four-watch system: ערב (evening), חצי הלילה (midnight), תרנגול קורא (rooster's call), בקר (morning). Greek has ὀψὲ ἢ μεσονυκτίου ἢ ἀλεκτοροφωνίας ἢ πρωΐ — the same four Roman night-watches. Both traditions agree on the four-fold division, but the Hebrew uses natural-language descriptions while the Greek uses more technical watch terminology.
translation_notes: אדון הבית (adon ha-bayit — 'master of the house', H113+H1004) — the Hebrew patriarchal household title, used here for the returning lord.

verses.translation: Lest when he comes{H935} he find{H4672} you sleeping{H3463}.
And what I say{H559} to you, to all{H3605} I say{H559}: Be awake{H5782}!

chapter_notes.summary: Mark 13 in Hebrew presents the Olivet Discourse with several dramatic divergences from the Greek TR. The most striking one-way markers include: (1) שקוץ שומם (v14) — Daniel's EXACT participial phrase for the desolating abomination, which a back-translator would not reproduce; (2) בן האלוה (v26) — 'Son of God' where Greek has 'Son of Man,' an irreconcilable divergence representing independent traditions; (3) המלכות שממיי (v10) — 'kingdom of heaven' where Greek has 'the gospel,' entirely different objects of proclamation; (4) כנפות הארץ (v27) — 'wings of the earth' (Isaiah 11:12) where Greek has 'four winds'; (5) חלו פני האל (v18) — the specific OT prayer-idiom 'entreat the face of God' where Greek has merely 'pray'; (6) השם (vv19-20) — the reverential 'the Name' for God, a characteristically Jewish practice. The Hebrew also frames eschatology differently: the world will 'perish/rot' (ליפסד, v4) rather than be 'completed'; the fig tree signals 'the end' (v28) rather than 'summer'; kings fight kings (v8) rather than kingdoms fighting kingdoms. Throughout, the Hebrew draws on Daniel, Isaiah, and Micah in ways that could not derive from the Greek text.
